title: Choosing your project and actually finishing it
promise: You'll choose the project you're going to take to the end, cut it down until it fits the time you have, and give it a delivery date with what has to exist by then. By the end you'll have the plan written and the first step done.
why: Most personal projects started on a course like this never get finished. And it's almost never for lack of knowledge: it's because something too big was chosen, with no date, and without having decided beforehand what the minimum is that counts as finished. By the third weekend the enthusiasm dips, a hard part appears, and the project stays in the folder. Nuria and Álvaro finished theirs for the same reason: both had cut their project in half before starting.

theory.title: A good project solves a problem you have
theory.text: The first mistake in choosing is looking for something impressive. A project that impresses but whose problem isn't yours gets abandoned the moment it turns difficult, because nothing pushes you to finish it. The project that gets finished is the one that takes a job you hate off your hands, or that solves something that annoyed you this very week. There you have three things money can't buy: you genuinely know the problem, you know when the solution is right, and you want the thing to exist. And along the way you can measure what it saves, which is what you needed for lessons 46 and 48.
theory.analogy: It's the difference between cooking for a photograph and cooking dinner. Dinner always gets finished, because at nine o'clock people have to eat.
theory.example: Álvaro didn't choose «an AI assistant for clinics». He chose «stop them ringing me to ask what time we open».

theory.title: The four filters before deciding
theory.text: When you have two or three candidates, run them through four questions. One: is the problem mine, or does it belong to someone close enough that I can ask when I'm unsure? Two: can I measure today how much it hurts, with a number? Three: can I test the hardest part in an afternoon, or does it depend on something outside my control? And four: do I already have what I need, or does someone have to give me permissions, access or data? That fourth filter is the one that sinks the most projects and the one people look at least: a project depending on someone else giving you something can sit still for a month with nothing you can do about it.
theory.example: «Automating the department's reports» fails filter four if the data lives in a system you don't have access to. Better to start with what you do have.
theory.analogy: Choosing where to go on holiday: it isn't the one that looks best in the photo, it's the one that fits the days you have, the money there is and who you're going with. The four filters get applied before booking, not after.

theory.title: Cutting it down until it fits
theory.text: Everyone picks a project three times bigger than they can finish. The way to fix that isn't working more: it's cutting before you start. Take your project and strip out everything that isn't essential for it to solve the problem once, for one person, in the simplest case. No exceptions, no odd cases, nothing pretty. What's left is the version you're going to build, and it's going to look slight to you: it has to. What you removed doesn't get thrown away, it goes on a later list. Most of that list you'll never do, and nothing will happen, because the project already worked without it.
theory.analogy: It's the single-lane bridge. If it works, you widen it. If you start with the four-lane one with a hard shoulder, nobody ever crosses.
theory.example: Nuria's project was «query all my documents». She cut it to «query my internal criteria, which are 40 files». She finished it in two weeks, and the rest came along almost by itself afterwards.

theory.title: The date before the scope
theory.text: A project with no date doesn't get finished, it gets abandoned. And the date isn't calculated from what has to be done, it gets set first and then the project gets cut until it fits. It's the opposite of what seems logical and it's what works, because with a fixed date the hard decisions actually get taken: what I remove, what I leave for later, what I do the simple way. Without a date, all those decisions get deferred and the project grows on its own. Set a real date, count the hours you're genuinely going to be able to give it (not the ones you'd like), and cut until the project fits in half those hours. The other half will be eaten by the things you didn't foresee.
theory.example: «Three weeks, two hours on Tuesdays and Thursdays and four on Saturdays: about 30 hours. I cut until the project fits in 15.»
theory.analogy: Dinner is at nine. You don't work that out by adding up how long each dish takes: you fix the time and then decide what to cook to make it. Otherwise you eat at eleven.

theory.title: Writing down what finished means
theory.text: «Finished» has to be written down before you start, or it never arrives: there's always something more to improve. It gets written as three to five sentences in the acceptance-criterion form you already know from block 08: what you do, what happens, within how long. The day those five sentences hold true, the project is finished even if it looks improvable to you. And that list has another job: it's what lets you say no to the new ideas that occur to you halfway through, which are what turn a three-week project into a seven-month one.
theory.example: «Finished is: I upload a new document and within 5 minutes I can query it; the 20 exam questions score 17 or more; and anyone can set it up following my start-up file.»
theory.analogy: The building work that's "nearly done" for four months. Without something signed saying what finished means, there's always one more skirting board.

theory.title: The hard part first
theory.text: The natural order is to start with what you know how to do, because it moves fast and feels good. It's a mistake, because the part that could sink the project is still sitting there waiting and you'll find out at the end, when there's no room left. The way that works is the other way round: identify the part you're unsure about, the one you don't know will work, and test it in the first few hours. If it works, the rest is familiar work. And if it doesn't work, you found out on day one and you can still change plan without having lost three weeks.
theory.example: Nuria didn't start by tidying documents. She started by uploading five to the Project and checking whether it answered citing the file. Half an hour, and with that she knew the project was viable.
theory.analogy: When you assemble flat-pack furniture, the piece that doesn't fit always turns up at the end, with the other twenty already in place. People who assemble a lot start by testing that piece.

tasks.title: Write three candidates and run them through the filters
tasks.action: Write three things you could build, each in a sentence starting with the problem and not with the technology. Run all three through the four filters: my problem or someone close, can be measured today, the hard part can be tested in an afternoon, and doesn't depend on permissions I don't have. Mark yes or no in each box.
tasks.expect: A table of three rows and four columns. Usually one wins clearly. If two tie, choose the one solving something that annoyed you this very week.
tasks.stuck: If three don't come to mind, look at last week and find what you did more than three times identically, or what you dreaded most. Your project is there.
tasks.prompt:
Help me choose between my candidate projects by running them through the four filters.

CANDIDATE 1: [one sentence starting with the problem, not the technology]
CANDIDATE 2: [same]
CANDIDATE 3: [same]
MY SITUATION: [how much time I have, what I can already do, who's nearby to ask]

Run all three through these four filters and score each 1 to 3, with one line of why:
1. Is the problem mine, or someone's nearby I can ask when I'm unsure?
2. Can I have something working, however ugly, in two weeks?
3. Do I already have the data or access needed, or am I depending on someone giving it to me?
4. Could I show it working in five minutes to someone non-technical?

Recommend one and say why, no ties. And warn me if any of the three sounds better than it is: the one that depends on a third party granting access is usually the one that never gets finished, however appealing it looks.

tasks.title: Set the date and count the real hours
tasks.where: In your calendar and on the sheet
tasks.action: Pick a specific delivery date, between two and four weeks away, and put it in the calendar as though it were an appointment with someone. Then count, slot by slot, the hours you'll genuinely be able to give it, looking at your real week, not your ideal one. Divide that total by two: that's your hours budget.
tasks.expect: A date and a number of hours that will look small to you. It is, deliberately: the other half will be eaten by the unforeseen, and if not, you finish early.
tasks.stuck: If you get fewer than ten hours, don't extend the date: cut the project further. A small project finished is worth infinitely more than a big one half-done.
tasks.prompt:
Help me set a date for my project and count the hours I actually have, not the ones I'd like to have.

MY PROJECT: [DESCRIBE IT IN ONE SENTENCE]
THE DATE I'M SETTING: [BETWEEN TWO AND FOUR WEEKS]
MY REAL WEEK: [working days, whether I have another job, which evenings I genuinely free up]

One: work out the hours I have between today and that date, pessimistically. Subtract what always falls over: a day when something comes up, end-of-week tiredness, the things that take twice as long.
Two: tell me how many real working hours that comes to, and compare it with what a project like mine usually takes.
Three: if the numbers don't add up, tell me now and don't soften it, and tell me what I cut: never the date.

And tell me how many hours to leave unplanned for what I haven't foreseen, because there's always something.

tasks.title: Cut it in half
tasks.action: Write down everything your project should do, unfiltered. Then split the list in two: what's essential for it to solve the problem once, for one person and in the simplest case; and everything else, which goes on a list called «later». Be hard: if in doubt, it goes to «later».
tasks.expect: Two lists, with the «later» one longer than the first. If your essential list has more than five items, cut again.
tasks.stuck: The trick for cutting: for each item on the list, ask whether the project is any use without it. If it is, it goes to «later». Almost everything is useful without almost everything.
tasks.prompt:
Help me cut my project in half, keeping what actually solves the problem.

EVERYTHING MY PROJECT SHOULD DO, UNFILTERED: [LIST IT]
THE PROBLEM IT SOLVES: [ONE SENTENCE]
HOURS I HAVE: [NUMBER]

Split the list in two: what's essential for it to solve the problem, and everything else. Be harsh: if something can be done by hand during the first version, it goes.

For each thing you cut, give me one line on why it can be lived without for now, so I can defend it if asked. And tell me what's left of the short list if even that doesn't fit: which single piece of functionality, if present, means I can show it and call it finished.

Warn me if cutting is killing what made the project interesting: that happens, and it's better to change project than to hand in a version that demonstrates nothing.

tasks.title: Write down what finished means
tasks.action: Three to five sentences in the block 08 format: when I do this, this happens, within this long. Make them checkable by someone other than you. And add a line at the end: «On [date], if these sentences hold true, the project is finished even if I think of improvements.»
tasks.expect: A short file you'll look at every time a new idea occurs to you mid-project. That's its main job.
tasks.stuck: If you don't know how to write a checkable sentence, look at the criteria in lesson 35. And if one of your sentences starts «that it looks good», that isn't a criterion: turn it into something you can look at.
tasks.prompt:
Help me write what finished means, before starting, so I'm not chasing a moving target.

MY PROJECT: [DESCRIBE IT]
THE ESSENTIALS LEFT AFTER CUTTING: [LIST]
WHO WILL SEE OR USE IT: [WHO]

Write me three to five sentences in the shape "when I do this, this happens, in under this long". Someone else has to be able to verify each one without asking me anything.

Rules: no "looks good" or "is usable". Nothing that depends on my opinion. And no sentence can start with "that it": each has to describe an action and a visible result.

At the end, tell me which sentence I'll be tempted to expand when the day comes, and tell me now that it doesn't get touched. That one decides whether the project gets finished or abandoned.

tasks.title: Attack the hard part today
tasks.action: Identify the part you're unsure about and test it today, however crudely and with made-up data. Don't build it properly: just check whether it's viable. Give yourself a two-hour limit and note the result: it works, it works with caveats, or it doesn't work.
tasks.expect: An answer to the question that could have sunk the project, in two hours rather than three weeks. If it's «it doesn't work», congratulations: you've just saved yourself the entire project and you're still in time to change it.
tasks.stuck: If you don't know which the hard part is, it's this question: which part of your project, if it doesn't work, makes everything else pointless? That one.
tasks.prompt:
Help me tackle the hard part of my project today, the part that could sink it.

MY PROJECT: [DESCRIBE IT]
THE PART I'M NOT SURE ABOUT: [DESCRIBE IT, however vaguely]
WHY I'M NOT SURE: [I don't know if it's possible, I don't know how, it depends on someone else…]

One: tell me exactly what question has to be answered today. Not "build that part": the yes-or-no question that, if the answer is no, changes the whole project.
Two: tell me how to test it in the crudest, fastest way possible, with made-up data and nothing built nicely. I want to settle the doubt in an afternoon, not construct anything.
Three: tell me what to do if the answer is no: what the alternative is, and at what point that means changing project.

Don't let me start with what I already know how to do, however much I'd rather: if this part doesn't work, everything else I build first is worthless.

tasks.title: Have the AI plan it by weeks and flag what's missing
tasks.action: With all the above written, ask for the breakdown and, above all, for what you've underestimated.
tasks.prompt:
I'm going to do a project and I want a realistic plan. I'm not a programmer and I work alone.

PROJECT: [one sentence, starting with the problem]
THE ESSENTIALS: [your short list]
WHAT FINISHED MEANS: [your sentences]
DELIVERY DATE: [date]
TOTAL HOURS AVAILABLE: [your number, already halved]
THE HARD PART, ALREADY TESTED: [what you tested and what happened]

GIVE ME:
1. The breakdown by week, with what has to exist at the end of each. Make each week end in something that works, even partly, not in a loose fragment.
2. Which task on my list I've underestimated and why. Be specific.
3. What I'd drop from the list if I'm halfway through with half the hours.
4. A warning: what's most likely to stop me finishing this.

Don't motivate me and don't give me general productivity advice.
tasks.expect: A plan by weeks and, most usefully, points 2 and 4. What always gets underestimated: preparing the data and writing the documentation.
tasks.stuck: If the plan comes out needing more hours than you have, don't accept it: say «I have half those hours, tell me what to drop» and apply what it says. Cutting is the skill of this lesson.

matters: That the project that gets finished is the one solving a problem of yours, not the one that impresses.
That the date gets set first and the scope gets cut until it fits, not the other way round.
That «finished» gets written before you start, or it never arrives.
That the hard part gets tested on day one, while you can still change plan.
ignore: Choosing a project for how well it will tell.
Planning with the hours you'd like to have.
The new ideas that occur to you halfway: they go on the later list.
canDo: Choose between candidates with four filters rather than by instinct.
Cut a project until it fits your real hours.
Know which day it's finished and not argue with yourself about it.
Find out on day one whether your project is viable.
cantDo: Finish a project that depends on permissions or data you don't have.
Know how long you'll really take the first time.
Stop new ideas appearing: only park them.
Finish something whose definition of finished isn't written down.
words: The essentials for solving the problem once, for one person, in the simplest case.
Where everything you cut goes. Almost none of it gets done, and nothing happens.
The real hours you can give it, divided by two.
The checkable sentences defining the end. They get written before you start.
The part that, if it doesn't work, leaves everything else pointless. It gets tested on day one.
next: That closes the programme: you know how to choose a tool, ask for things properly, set up your environment, code with company, automate, build agents, connect your data, check it works, protect it and hand it over. What's left isn't another lesson: it's doing your project and finishing it on the day you put in the calendar.
